newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil deputies paid to vote for reelection-paper.
newsitem.headline: Brazil deputies paid to vote for reelection-paper.

text.p: Five congressmen from the northern Brazilian state of Acre were allegedly paid off to vote in favor of a constitutional amendment allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for re-election, a newspaper reported on Tuesday.

The lead story in Folha de Sao Paulo said the daily possessed taped telephone conversations between Deputy Ronivon Santiago and another unidentified person in which Santiago allegedly admits to receiving 200,000 reais ($188,679) for his vote.

In the purported recordings, Santiago allegedly said the governors of Acre and the state of Amazonas, Orleir Cameli and Amazonino Mendes, paid off another four deputies from Acre so they would vote in favor of re-election. They all received 200,000 reais each, according to Santiago.

Governor Cameli and three of the deputies have denied the accusations and Governor Mendes and Deputy Santiago were unavailable for comment, Folha de Sao Paulo said. Only one deputy allegedly admitted being offered money, but said he did not take any, Folha said.
None of the deputies were available Tuesday morning to comment on the matter. A presidential spokesman said he was unable to comment and it was really up to the governors to make a statement.
Government Chief of Staff Clovis Carvalho told Folha de Sao Paulo the government was wholly unaware of the matter.

"Obviously this has nothing to do with the actions of the federal government," Folha quoted Carvalho as saying in its exclusive three-page spread story. "We would never do or even imagine to do something like that."
He said he did not think the affair would hamper the Senate vote on the re-election bill.
The re-election amendment not only benefits President Cardoso, but also gives governors and mayors a second chance to run for office.

During the re-election vote in the Chamber of Deputies six of the chamber's eight deputies from Acre voted in favor of the amendment, which was approved by 336 votes in favor in the first round of voting January 28 and by 368 votes in the second round February 25.
All the deputies are from the government-allied Liberal Front Party (PFL) except one who is a member of Brazil's biggest party the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB).
((--Simona de Logu, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
